source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles Reveal Fundamental Limits of Machine Insight (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Insight-like riddles (impasse, restructuring) were tested on 38 LLMs, zero-shot, no retrieval. Most models were far below humans.
numbers: Human subset n=126, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2) on 120 items. Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. GPT-5 fell inside the human CI.
limits: Human data from a pilot sample; no model-by-model test; riddles are public so contamination is possible.
agent_relevance: Plain LLMs fail insight-type restructuring far more than humans. Reasoning mode helps but does not close the gap.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: reasoning vs non-reasoning odds
finding: On all 201 riddles, reasoning models beat non-reasoning models by a clear margin. Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did.
numbers: Odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99-2.64, p<0.0001). Population accuracy 9.42% vs 19.25%.
limits: Observational. Confounded by release date and training recipe.
agent_relevance: System design and training matter more than size for insight-like tasks. A deliberate-thinking mode is a lever, not a cure.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: verification failure
finding: Models often wrote the correct answer in their thought log but did not endorse it, then answered wrongly. Generation and evaluation separate, like a failed feeling-of-rightness.
numbers: Verification failures were 5.23% (Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview) to 39.34% (Grok 4) of wrong answers. DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%, Claude Opus 4 25.00%. Detected by literal gold-answer match in the log.
quote: models generate a correct intermediate candidate but fail to endorse it as their final answer
limits: Literal string match; only 4 models had usable logs; logs may not be faithful.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit endorse-or-reject step with a stopping rule after a candidate appears. The comparison stage of the three-process view maps here.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: language of thought log
finding: Reasoning in Japanese or English did not reliably change accuracy. Authors also describe 'false insight': confident commitment to a wrong reframing.
numbers: Grok-4: Japanese 29.5% (33/112) vs English 48.8% (40/82), Fisher p=0.0071. Claude Opus 4: 36.7% vs 28.7%, p=0.356. Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0/12 vs 22/188, p=0.369.
limits: Language of the log is chosen by the model, so it is confounded with item difficulty.
agent_relevance: Surface language is not the bottleneck. Restructuring and evaluation are.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Tested whether mid-trace 'Aha' shifts (Wait, re-evaluate) in GRPO-tuned Qwen2.5 and Llama models raise accuracy. They are rare and mostly do not.
numbers: 1M+ traces, 3 domains (cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, Rush Hour). Shifts in 6.31% of traces pooled (about 7.6% for Qwen2.5-1.5B). Accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces, N=723,200. Shift rate did not rise with training.
quote: reasoning shifts are symptoms of unstable inference behavior rather than an intrinsic mechanism for self-correction
limits: Mainly small models (Qwen2.5-1.5B, plus 7B/8B). Shifts are detected by lexical and structural markers, which can mislabel hesitations.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous 'insight' in a chain of thought is a symptom of unstable inference, not a reliable solver. Do not rely on the model to restructure itself.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) entropy-gated reconsideration
finding: Externally forcing a reconsideration cue when token entropy is high improved accuracy, even though spontaneous shifts did not.
numbers: MATH-500 +8.41 percentage points (0.322 to 0.406); crosswords +0.45pp; Rush Hour +0.01pp. High-entropy bucket = top 20% by Pass-1 sequence entropy.
limits: Small gains outside math. Small-model scale. Gains come from an extrinsic trigger.
agent_relevance: Code-side impasse detector (entropy or low confidence) that triggers a forced second pass. An extrinsic version of the analytic override in dual-process accounts.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) shift effect varies by domain and temperature
finding: The effect of shifts depends on domain and decoding temperature. Near zero on Rush Hour; harmful on Math in the raw contrast.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B accuracy step 0 to after training: crosswords 7.69 to 10.00, Math 31.00 to 35.00. Temperatures 0, 0.05, 0.3, 0.7. Math raw shift contrast -18.35pp in one reported condition.
limits: Raw contrast differs from fixed-effects estimates; sign changes with setting.
agent_relevance: A reconsideration trigger must be tested per task type; it is not uniformly good.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT (Nature Comput Sci 3:833)
finding: Ten OpenAI models on 150 Cognitive Reflection Test items plus semantic illusions. Larger pre-ChatGPT models gave the intuitive wrong answer more often than humans. ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 avoided the trap.
numbers: Humans n=455: CRT 38% correct (original study 41%, n=3,428); 55% intuitive. GPT-3-davinci family 70-90% intuitive, davinci-003 5% correct. ChatGPT-3.5 59% correct, 15% intuitive. ChatGPT-4 96% correct, 0% intuitive.
limits: CRT items may be in training data; authors warn against equating model and human cognition.
agent_relevance: Dual-process vocabulary fits older LLMs. Strong chat models look different: fast and right.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) chain of thought as System 2, Study 2
finding: Instructing davinci-003 to think step by step raised correctness and cut intuitive errors. Blocking chain of thought in ChatGPT barely hurt it.
numbers: davinci-003: CoT 0% to 100%, correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. ChatGPT-3.5 CoT 97% to 0%, correct change not significant (p=.49). ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: The instruction to suppress reasoning may be imperfectly obeyed.
agent_relevance: Written step-by-step reasoning works as an analytic override for weak models. For strong ones the gain on trap items is small.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) in-context examples build intuition, Studies 3 and 5
finding: Worked examples of same-type tasks lifted davinci-003 to high accuracy without chain of thought, like practice in humans.
numbers: CRT type 2: 2% to 92% after 2 examples. Type 3: 12% to 92% after 7. Type 1: 0% to about 78% after 30. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for 72%; ChatGPT-4 88% correct.
limits: Same-type items are alike, so the model may learn a surface rule.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples act like trained intuition. The schema can store solved analogues as primes.

source: Yax, Anllo and Palminteri (2024) Studying and improving reasoning in humans and machines
finding: Fresh CRT-style items (to avoid memorised originals) given to GPT-3 variants and 100 humans. Models showed intuitive errors, and more refined models were more intuitive-prone, not less.
numbers: New CRT items: GPT-3 mean correct 0.11, intuitive 0.35. davinci-003 correct 0.14 vs humans 0.46 (n=100); davinci-003 intuitive 0.45 vs humans 0.33. Math-only versions: davinci-003 correct 0.55, humans 0.69.
limits: Older GPT-3 family only; temperature 0.7, 100 repeats.
agent_relevance: Memorised trap items overstate model ability. Use new variants when testing.

source: Yax et al. (2024) prompting effects, humans vs machines
finding: A prompt telling the model to reason, or showing an example, raised correct answers in davinci-003 but not in humans.
numbers: Reasoning prompt: correct +0.18 (P<.0001), intuitive -0.02 (ns). Example prompt: correct +0.14 (P<.0001). In humans the reasoning prompt was numerically negative (ns); human answers 126 vs 11.4 characters, versus davinci-003 257 vs 69.5.
limits: Humans may not have complied; online sample.
agent_relevance: Cheap analytic-mode prompts work on models; do not assume the human result transfers.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 on 12 vignette tasks plus task-based tests. It gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three standard CRT items; small rewording of vignettes produced non-human mistakes.
numbers: Standard CRT 1-3: 3 of 3 intuitive-wrong. Of 12 vignettes, 6 answered correctly and all 12 correct or human-like in the standard form.
limits: Early GPT-3; vignettes may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Vignette success may be memory. Test with perturbed items.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for LLMs (EMNLP)
finding: 1,100 multiple-choice puzzles that need breaking default commonsense (sentence and word puzzles), with semantic and context rewrites to test consistency.
numbers: Human 92% (102 items, 3 experts); ChatGPT 53% and 63% on the two subtasks; random 25%. Group-based accuracy (original plus rewrites) was much lower than instance accuracy for models; human group-based stayed high.
limits: Multiple-choice; some word puzzles may be memorised; experts, not random adults.
agent_relevance: Models can solve the original puzzle yet fail the reworded one, so the answer was not grounded in restructuring.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9 BRAINTEASER overview
finding: 483 submissions from 182 participants. Fine-tuning and prompting (few-shot, CoT, ensembles) pushed the top systems to 100% on the held-out 20% subset.
numbers: Best systems 100% on both subtasks. Table rows: human 0.920 (sentence original), GPT-4 0.858 on the subset vs 0.898 on the full benchmark.
limits: Top systems may exploit regularities in the puzzle family; authors say the consistency gap remains.
agent_relevance: Benchmark saturation by tuning and scaffolds does not show insight. Use consistency metrics.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LatEval: interactive lateral thinking puzzles (LREC-COLING)
finding: Interactive situation-puzzle game: the model asks yes/no questions of a host and must deduce the hidden story. Most LLMs did badly, GPT-4 best.
numbers: Over 2,000 puzzles. English, GPT-4 as host: AC 34.2, QR 58.4, QD 79.8, AT 10.2 for GPT-4 as player. GPT-3.5 AC 17.1; Claude AC 14.5; Bloomchat-176B AC 1.8.
limits: GPT-4 grades GPT-4, so self-preference risk, though authors report human correlation.
agent_relevance: Asking divergent questions is a separate skill from deducing. Divergent question generation could be a dedicated step at impasse.

source: Ganapini et al. (2021) Thinking Fast and Slow in AI: the Role of Metacognition (SOFAI)
finding: Proposes SOFAI: fast solvers reuse past experience; slow solvers are activated by a metacognitive module when needed. Position paper with a multi-agent architecture.
numbers: No benchmark numbers in this paper; architecture only.
limits: Proposal paper. Not tested on insight problems.
agent_relevance: The metacognitive switch between fast and slow is the same job as our impasse detector.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking
finding: A small fine-tuned model (Swift) acts quickly. A large LLM (Sage) plans and grounds when a heuristic detects trouble. Tested on ScienceWorld.
numbers: 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.7 average score vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3. Fewer tokens per action.
limits: One text environment. The switching rule is hand-built.
agent_relevance: A working dual-process loop inside an LLM agent, with a code-side rule deciding when to go slow.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Slow multi-step methods (Rephrase and Respond, System 2 Attention, Branch-Solve-Merge) were distilled into direct answers by fine-tuning. Often kept the gain at far lower cost.
numbers: Last-letter task: Llama-2-70B-chat 30.0%; 2-step RaR 39.5%; distilled 98.0%. Coin flip: 56.1% base; RaR variants 58.5% and 77.2%; distilled 75.69%. S2A task: System 1 51.6%, S2A 76.0%, distilled 81.3%.
limits: Chain-of-thought arithmetic did not distill: about 7% accuracy for distilled System 2 on the math set. Needs tasks where the slow output is learnable.
agent_relevance: Boundary: some analytic procedures compile into intuition, but not step-by-step arithmetic. The scaffold should not assume compression.

source: Su et al. (2025) Dualformer: controllable fast and slow thinking (ICLR)
finding: One transformer trained on randomly truncated reasoning traces can answer in fast, slow or auto mode.
numbers: 30x30 maze: slow mode 97.6% optimal vs Searchformer 93.3% with 45.5% fewer steps; fast mode 80% vs solution-only 30%; auto mode 96.6% with 59.9% fewer steps.
limits: Maze and math tasks; no insight problems.
agent_relevance: One model can switch depth by mode; dropping parts of traces trains robustness.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention
finding: Have the model rewrite the context to strip irrelevant or opinionated text before answering. This is selective encoding done by an LLM.
numbers: Factual QA with opinion: LLaMA-2-70B-chat 62.8% vs S2A 80.3% (oracle 82.0%). Math with distractors: 51.7% to 61.3%.
limits: Costs an extra generation; fails if the rewrite drops needed facts.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of Davidson and Sternberg's selective encoding. A pre-filter step on the framing can raise accuracy.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) DPT-Agent: Dual Process Theory in a language agent framework
finding: Agent with System 1 (finite-state machine plus code-as-policy) and System 2 (theory of mind plus asynchronous reflection) for real-time human-AI collaboration.
numbers: Abstract reports significant gains over single-system baselines in simultaneous cooperative tasks; table values not extracted.
limits: Real-time game setting; not insight tasks.
agent_relevance: Shows a fast code layer plus slow reflection used in a deployed loop.

source: Davidson and Sternberg (1984) The role of insight in intellectual giftedness
finding: Three-process theory: insight comes from selective encoding, selective combination and selective comparison. Gifted children did better on insight items.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: From memory. No LLM test of this theory was found.
agent_relevance: Maps onto three steps: pick relevant facts, combine them, compare with known analogues.

source: Wiley and Danek (2024) insight research review (cited by the NazoNazo paper)
finding: Cited in the NazoNazo paper as the current review of insight; human insight scores are often bimodal.
numbers: Not opened. NazoNazo human scores out of 20 were bimodal with peaks at 0 and 20.
limits: Citation only; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Use as the human baseline when comparing models.

source: Search gap: no LLM study of three-process theory found
finding: Three web searches (the budget ran out) and arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs (rate limited) found no paper that tests selective encoding, combination and comparison in LLMs by name.
numbers: 0 direct hits among about 30 result titles seen.
limits: Search was limited by rate limits; a gap is not proven.
agent_relevance: Treat this subfield as background. The dual-process engineering evidence is the usable part.
